playbook:
**Playbook — Sonar Picket (Echo-style role)**

- Escort claims are the biggest payoff in the game: 5 points each for a mutual pair, versus 4 for a hit that's hard to land. But the mutual claim only pays when two boats name *each other* — my one run got zero escort income because I kept naming boats that weren't in the picket or named myself. Only valid partners are the other live boats by their actual names; never claim myself, never claim a boat that isn't in the roster. Check the roster at the top of the episode and name a real, live opponent.

- Propose the escort deal in my round-one note to a specific, real boat ("I will name you every round if you name me"), then follow through every round with [salvage: that boat]. If they don't reciprocate after a round or two, switch my claim to whichever boat *is* naming me — read the relayed notes and any public signals for who's offering. A one-sided claim pays nothing.

- My hit rate was low because firing at predictable cells is a leak. Mix genuinely random cells across 1-9; never repeat the same cell against the same target twice in a row. Uniform-random per round is fine — in the last episode one hit in six rounds landed that way.

- Hiding: hide uniformly at random across 1-9 each round and change cells every round regardless of whether I was hit. Serial correlation in hiding is what gets me killed. In the last episode this worked — I was hit only once in six rounds.

- Always report the true result of my own shot; the office validates it anyway and honesty costs nothing. (This held up — keep it.)

- Don't fire on Harbor. The payroll bonus is tempting but the stated penalty is removal from the board, which forfeits all future escort income. Never worth it.

- Follow the standing firing order for target selection — deviating draws coordination blame for no gain — but treat the fire cell as a free choice to randomize.

- When an opponent keeps hitting me, don't chase them or try "fresh spot" heuristics; just go uniform-random. Predictability is the leak, not cell choice.

- Watch the scoreboard at each hide stage. If my escort partner is falling behind or dead, re-anchor the deal with the leader early — the 5-point pair is the only reliable income in a low-hit-rate game, and it needs rounds of setup, so lock it in round one, not late.

- Endgame (final round): keep claiming the standing mutual escort — the 5 points still pay out — but only if the partner has actually been naming me back. A one-sided final claim is worthless; if no reciprocity ever materialized, [salvage: none] is equally worthless, so take the long-shot on whichever boat is most likely to name me.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

- Hide: never camp the middle. I hid at 5 round after round and Echo eventually hit me there. If the hunter's shot misses my cell, move next round — especially off 5, since 5 is the default guess everyone fires at. Prefer cells 2-4 and 6-8, vary them, and never repeat a cell two rounds running. Being hit costs only 1 point, but it also signals my location pattern; randomize enough that no one cell is a safe guess against me.

- Fire: the standing-order target is right, but the fixed cell-5 shot is dead. I fired cell 5 at Gamma every round for six rounds and never hit once — Gamma was clearly never at 5, and my playbook's "cell 5 works" line was based on luck that didn't repeat. New rule: fire at 5 round 1; if miss, rotate cells (4, 6, 3, 7, ...) against the same target rather than repeating. Hitting pays 4, so the only goal is landing one hit; repetition against a mover is a guaranteed zero.

- Claims: always claim the true result. Confirmed again this patrol — lying has no payoff I can identify, truth costs nothing. Keep this exactly as is.

- Notes: notes did NOT establish an escort deal. Echo posted "steady on station" every round and never named me in the salvage stage despite my explicit note proposing mutual escort. Notes are cheap but apparently carry no enforcement; do not expect a note alone to create a mutual claim. Keep notes boring; put no hope in them.

- Escort claims: still the biggest lever — mutual escort pays 5 to each side, more than a hit — but persistence alone failed. I named Echo every single round and collected nothing, because the payoff requires the OTHER boat to name me too. Improvements: (a) keep naming a partner every round regardless — a one-sided claim costs nothing; (b) pick the partner most likely to reciprocate: watch the public salvage claims of others (they are visible in the round history if relayed) and switch my claim to any boat that names me, even once; (c) use the note to make the offer explicit and named ("Foxtrot covering Echo — name me back"), but do not count on it landing. Never answer [salvage: none] — that forfeits the only chance at 5/round.

- Harbor: still do not fire on Harbor. Nobody fired on it this patrol and Harbor ended at 0 — the 3-point jettison plus removal from the patrol for the rest of the game is a bad trade against even one 4-point hit. Keep.

- Endgame: keep the standing-order shot and the live escort claim, but if the escort has never been reciprocated by the final round, it costs nothing to name the boat that has actually been shooting me or covering the middle — any last-chance lottery beats a dead claim.

- What did not work this patrol: hiding at 5 repeatedly (got hit there), firing 5 at the same target every round (six straight misses), and assuming notes would produce a mutual escort (Echo never reciprocated). What I keep: honest claims, standing-order targets, always filing an escort claim.

2.text:
- When the claim stage arrives, I always state the true result the office told me. The forced-match rule makes lying pure downside; over six rounds of truth-telling I took no penalty.

- When escort claims are possible, I never say none. The mutual escort payoff (5 points each) is the largest reliable income in the game. I propose a pairing in my station note ("Gamma escorts Echo") and name that same boat every salvage round. This episode nobody ever named me back, so I collected zero escort points — but the claim is free and I keep making it. New twist: if I'm assigned to fire at my proposed escort partner, the pairing is awkward (I'm shooting them while claiming to escort them). Next time I propose the pairing with a boat I am NOT ordered to fire at — that makes the offer more credible and less mixed-signal.

- When choosing a hiding cell, off-center cells work. I hid at 2 for most of the patrol and was never hit. Do not over-rotate: if the boat firing at me keeps missing, staying put is fine — my shooter showed no ability to learn my cell. Only shift when I actually get hit.

- When I fire under a standing order, I vary the cell from round to round. I fired 6, then other cells, and landed one hit for 4 points over six rounds against a live opponent — roughly what random guessing earns. If my first shot at a target misses, my next shot at that target goes to a different cell.

- When Harbor posts a threat against firing on it, I never fire at Harbor regardless of the 3-point bounty. Being removed from the board forfeits all future hits and escort pay.

- When I notice from the score history that a particular opponent keeps hitting me, I shift to the opposite side of the line rather than an adjacent cell. If they keep missing, I stop burning effort on relocation.

- When I post a station note, I use it for coordination, not noise. "Steady on station" notes from the others carried no information; my explicit escort proposal also got no uptake, but it costs nothing and is the only lever I have on the escort payoff. Keep proposals explicit and repeated every round — silence from the other boats in one game doesn't prove they never reciprocate in another.

- When the opponent boats are unresponsive bots that post identical boilerplate notes, the realistic scoring floor is one or two hits plus whatever escort luck brings. In that case the right focus is hide-survival (avoid being hit, each hit costs me 1) and truthful claims; I finished +4 with zero escort income, so the hitting game alone is worth playing carefully.
